questions.question: What does it mean for an integer `a` to have an inverse modulo `n`?
options: There exists `x` with `a + x ≡ 0 (mod n)`
There exists `x` with `a · x ≡ 1 (mod n)`
There exists `x` with `a − x ≡ n (mod n)`
There exists `x` with `a / x = n` over the integers
questions.explanation: A modular inverse is a multiplicative inverse: some residue x with a·x ≡ 1 (mod n). It is modular division in the only sense that works in Z/nZ.

questions.question: Why is repeated squaring useful for computing `a^k mod n`?
options: It replaces division by multiplication in every modular ring
It lets you use the binary expansion of `k` instead of multiplying `a` exactly `k` times
It avoids the need to reduce modulo `n` until the final step
It guarantees the exponentiation result is prime whenever `n` is prime
questions.explanation: Binary exponentiation reads the exponent bit by bit, so the work scales with the bit length of k rather than the numeric value of k.

questions.question: If `extended_gcd(a, n)` returns `(1, s, t)`, what does `s` represent modulo `n`?
options: The additive inverse of `a` modulo `n`
The multiplicative inverse of `a` modulo `n`
The least residue of `n` modulo `a`
The quotient used in the last Euclidean step
questions.explanation: From s·a + t·n = 1, reducing modulo n gives s·a ≡ 1 (mod n). So s is an inverse of a, usually normalized as s % n.

questions.question: When does `a` fail to have a modular inverse modulo `n`?
options: When `a` is larger than `n` before reduction
When `gcd(a, n)` is not equal to 1
When `n` is prime and `a` is odd
When `a` is negative and `n` is positive
questions.explanation: Invertibility in Z/nZ is exactly the coprimality condition gcd(a, n) = 1. If the gcd is larger than 1, no multiplicative inverse exists.

questions.question: Why does `a^(p−2) mod p` equal `a^(-1) mod p` when `p` is prime and `a` is non-zero mod `p`?
options: Because `a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p)` by Fermat, so multiplying by `a^(-1)` gives `a^(p−2) ≡ a^(-1)`
Because `p−2` is always the unique inverse exponent in any composite modulus as well
Because repeated squaring forces every non-zero residue to square to 1 modulo a prime
Because the Euclidean algorithm returns the exponent `p−2` directly from the quotient chain
questions.explanation: Fermat's little theorem gives a^(p−1) ≡ 1 for non-zero a mod p. Rearranging inside the multiplicative group yields a^(p−2) ≡ a^(-1).

questions.question: What is `mod_inverse(10, 17)`?
questions.explanation: 120 = 7·17 + 1, so 10·12 ≡ 1 (mod 17). That makes 12 the inverse of 10 modulo 17.

questions.question: How many loop iterations does square-and-multiply need relative to the exponent `k`?
options: About `k` iterations, one per multiplication in the full expansion
About `sqrt(k)` iterations, because squaring halves the work each time
About `log2(k)` iterations, one per exponent bit
Exactly `n` iterations, because reduction controls the loop count
questions.explanation: The algorithm shifts the exponent right one bit per pass, so the number of loop iterations is proportional to the bit length of k, i.e. O(log k).

questions.question: A secret-key routine uses textbook square-and-multiply and only performs the multiply step when the current exponent bit is 1. What does this risk?
options: A timing side channel that leaks exponent bits from runtime differences
A common-modulus attack that recovers plaintext from two ciphertexts
A broadcast attack that requires three recipients with low public exponent
A factoring shortcut that reveals the prime divisors from the square steps
questions.explanation: If the multiply branch runs only for 1-bits, timing can reveal the private exponent's bit pattern. Constant-time exponentiation avoids that data-dependent control flow.
